> 豫兮若冬涉川；猶兮若畏四鄰；儼兮其若客；渙兮其若凌釋；敦兮其若樸；曠兮其若谷；混兮其若濁.

Chapter 15 is the most detailed portrait of a person in the whole book. It does not say what such a person does. It says what he looks like standing there.

Seven images, and almost every reading turns them into a list of virtues: cautious, respectful, simple, humble. That is the wrong direction, because most of these characters were not moral compliments in Laozi's time. They described states of a mind in operation.

Put them back in their period and the seven become seven negatives — seven ways of not doing something.

## 豫 and 猶: the two hesitant animals

豫 and 猶 are animals in the old vocabulary: 豫 is a kind of elephant, 猶 a kind of monkey, both known for pausing before they move. 若冬涉川 — like crossing a river in winter, testing the ice before each step.

The modern reading, "cautious," softens it into a personality trait. What the image actually shows is a specific relation to risk: not fear of the ice, but attention to it. The person is not hesitating because he is timid; he is hesitating because he is reading the surface.

## 儼兮其若客

Solemn, as if a guest. 客 is the key: a guest is in someone else's house. He uses the room, he eats the meal, he does not rearrange the furniture or claim the title.

This is the same 租客 logic as chapter 10, rendered as posture rather than principle. The person who is 若客 does not have to announce that he is not the owner; it shows in how he sits.

## 渙兮其若凌釋

Loose, as if ice were melting. 凌釋 is the moment when frozen water lets go — the tension releasing, not because it was forced, but because the temperature changed.

This is the one image in the set that is about un-clenching. Most people carry a held state — jaw, shoulders, attention — and treat it as normal. The image says: the thaw is the natural state; the freeze was the exception.

## 敦兮其若樸 / 曠兮其若谷 / 混兮其若濁

樸 is unworked timber — the log before the carpenter. Not "simple" as an aesthetic, but unmade: no finish applied, no shape imposed yet.

谷 is the valley again: empty and therefore able to receive.

濁 is turbid water. This one is easy to misread as a flaw. But the image is of water that has been stirred and not yet settled — it contains everything, and it is not pretending to be clear.

## 孰能濁以靜之徐清？孰能安以動之徐生？

Two questions, and they are the chapter's actual instruction.

Who can let the turbid settle, slowly, into clarity? Who can let the settled move, slowly, into life?

徐 — slowly — is doing the work in both. The failure is not turbidity or stillness; it is forcing the transition. Shake the muddy water and it stays muddy. Leave still water still forever and it stagnates.

## 不欲盈

> 保此道者，不欲盈。夫唯不盈，故能蔽而新成.

The last line explains the whole portrait. 不欲盈 — not wanting to be full. Not a modesty rule: a full vessel cannot receive, and a full person cannot be corrected.

蔽而新成 — worn, and therefore able to become new. The old finish has to wear off before a new one can take. This is the only chapter in the book where being used-up is presented as an advantage.
